content.title: Career Growth Control Boundary
content.text:
The Eduversal Career Growth Framework and the Master Role Register govern Career Growth roles. They govern role approval, progression, appointment, governance/reporting boundaries, and teaching-hour/allowance values. This Section 12 governs the wider staff lifecycle and how HR work is carried out. It does not create Career Growth roles, reporting authority, or promotion entitlements. Formal appraisal evidence may support progression decisions. However, induction records, coaching notes, mentoring records, and Subject Specialist developmental observations remain formative, unless an explicitly authorized process states otherwise.

Framework: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1YwUbe38KrT2-vkxZsRFcSPj7cPuE3f1D0mUl1t4KNLs/edit

Master Role Register: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1j9V-3WfqA6eYl4R3SawgDdvY5lDv-SZM5ah153aGWko/edit

The quality of education in any school depends above all on the quality of its teachers and staff. At Eduversal Partner Schools, we know that attracting, developing, and keeping excellent educators is central to our mission. Our mission is to deliver world-class Cambridge International education, uphold Indonesian values, and prepare students for global success.

This section gives a full framework for managing the whole staff lifecycle in all Eduversal Partner Schools in Indonesia. It covers the special context of our schools. We deliver Cambridge Primary, Lower Secondary, IGCSE, and AS & A Level programs. We also teach Indonesian national curriculum subjects (Pendidikan Pancasila, Bahasa Indonesia, Religion, and Civics). We serve diverse student populations, including students who learn English as an extra language. Our schools work in many settings: urban and rural locations, day schools, boarding schools, and Islamic boarding schools.
Managing the staff lifecycle well serves several important purposes:

items: Quality Assurance: Making sure all staff have the qualifications, skills, and professional attitudes required to deliver high-quality Cambridge education and meet Indonesian regulatory standards.
Student Outcomes: Improving student learning, wellbeing, and achievement directly, through good teaching, pastoral care, and support services.
Continuous Improvement: Building a professional culture where staff get support and development, and are able to grow throughout their careers.
Compliance and Accreditation: Meeting Indonesian employment law requirements, Cambridge Centre standards, and CIS/WASC accreditation criteria for professional staffing.
Retention and Morale: Creating positive workplaces where talented educators choose to build their careers and help improve the school over the long term.
content.title: Purpose of Comprehensive Staff Lifecycle Management

content.text: Research consistently shows that teacher quality is the single most important school-based factor in student achievement. At Eduversal Partner Schools, we see this directly in our Quality Management System (QMS) data. The data shows strong links between three things: teacher appraisal ratings, professional development engagement, and student performance on internal assessments (EASE) and Cambridge examinations. Good staff members help students succeed by:

items: Delivering engaging, well-planned lessons that promote deep learning and critical thinking
Providing differentiated support for diverse learners, including EAL students and those with special educational needs
Creating safe, inclusive, and positive classroom environments where all students can thrive
Building strong relationships with students that support their academic, social, and emotional development
Using assessment data carefully to guide teaching and intervention
Modeling the Eduversal Schoolwide Learner Outcomes (SLOs) and Profil Pelajar Pancasila competencies in their professional practice
content.title: Link Between Staff Quality and Student Outcomes

content.text: Staff lifecycle management is directly aligned with the Eduversal mission. Our mission is to provide excellent international education. This education develops globally competent, ethically grounded graduates who do well academically and contribute meaningfully to society. Every part of recruitment, induction, appraisal, and professional development is designed so that staff show and advance our six Schoolwide Learner Outcomes:

steps: Academic Excellence: Staff have deep subject knowledge and teaching expertise to prepare students for Cambridge qualifications and Indonesian national assessments.
Communication: Staff model good communication in more than one language (English and Bahasa Indonesia). They support students' language development in all subjects.
Global Competence: Staff bring international perspectives and celebrate cultural diversity. They prepare students to engage with global issues.
Ethical Leadership: Staff show integrity, professionalism, and ethical decision-making. They are role models for students.
Innovation and Creativity: Staff use new teaching strategies, use technology well, and encourage creative problem-solving.
Wellbeing: Staff put students' mental health, safety, and whole-person development first. They create supportive learning environments.
content.title: Alignment with School Mission and Schoolwide Learner Outcomes

content.text: Eduversal Partner Schools are committed to building a professional culture of continuous improvement, collaboration, and mutual support. This culture rests on several basic principles:

items: Growth Mindset: We believe all staff can develop their practice through focused effort, quality feedback, and ongoing learning.
Reflective Practice: Teachers regularly reflect on their teaching and analyze student data. They make changes based on evidence to improve outcomes.
Collaborative Learning: Professional Learning Communities (PLCs), peer observations, and mentoring help staff learn from one another and share good practice.
Evidence-Based Decision Making: Data guides professional development and improvement work. This data comes from the Appraisal Program, EASE assessments, Cambridge exam results, and school-wide KPIs.

Developmental Approach to Evaluation: Our appraisal system focuses on growth and support, not punishment. We recognize that good teachers develop over time with high-quality feedback and targeted professional development.
content.title: Professional Culture and Continuous Improvement Mindset

content.text: The Development of Teaching Proficiency (DTP) program and the Appraisal Program are central to this culture of continuous improvement. Eduversal delivers both through its Educamp platform. Through regular observations, coaching, workshops, and shared planning, we make sure every staff member can strengthen their practice and advance their career. The following sections give detailed guidance on each phase of the staff lifecycle, from recruitment to exit. This guidance helps Principals and HR teams build and keep excellent teams of educators.

Strategic workforce planning makes sure that schools have the right number of qualified staff in the right roles at the right time. This forward-looking approach supports continuity, quality, and responsible spending across Eduversal Partner Schools.
Each school carries out a full staffing review at least once a year (usually in Term 3, for the following academic year). The review includes:

items: Enrollment Projections: Analysis of current enrollment, expected student numbers by year group, and expected growth or decline. Data sources include application trends, student retention rates, and population patterns in the school's catchment area.

Class Size Planning: Deciding the best class sizes. They align with Cambridge recommendations (typically 20-24 students for Primary, 20-24 for Lower Secondary, 18-20 for IGCSE practical subjects, 14-18 for AS & A Level). They also align with Indonesian regulations (maximum 28 for Primary, 32 for Secondary).

Curriculum Requirements: Assessment of teaching loads in all subjects. This includes Cambridge international subjects and Indonesian national curriculum subjects (Pancasila, Bahasa Indonesia, Religion, Civics). It also includes specialist areas (EAL support, SEN, library, counseling, extracurricular coordination).

Subject Expertise Gaps: Finding subjects where extra expertise is needed. This applies especially to specialized Cambridge qualifications (e.g., Further Mathematics, Computer Science, specific language options, Design & Technology).
Support Staff Needs: Review of the administrative, technical, boarding, and facility staff the school needs for smooth operations.

content.text: Note: The General Manager (GM) or Foundation Representative oversees compliance with these standards across the Eduversal network. Schools that find it hard to recruit staff who meet the minimum qualifications should consult the GM before making offers.
Eduversal Partner Schools aim to keep staff-student ratios that balance educational quality with sustainable operations:

items: Overall School Ratio: Target 1:10 (including all academic staff and leadership)
Early Years: 1:8-10 (teacher-student) with classroom assistants
Primary (Years 1-6): 1:10-12 average class size; specialist teachers for PE, Music, Art
Lower Secondary (Grades 7-8): 1:20-24 average class size; subject specialist teachers
IGCSE (Grades 9-10): 1:18-24 depending on subject; smaller for practical subjects (Science, Design, ICT)
AS & A Level (Grades 11-12): 1:8-16 to allow individual support and university preparation
Support Staff: EAL support (1:40-60 EAL learners), SEN support (1:30-50 students), Counselors (1:200-300 students), Librarian (1 per school minimum)
content.title: Staff-Student Ratios

content.text: These ratios are guidelines. Actual staffing decisions consider school size, student needs, the curriculum offered, and budget limits. Schools with large numbers of EAL or SEN students may require extra support staff.

International schools usually have higher staff turnover than local schools, because expatriate teachers often move between countries. Good succession planning reduces disruption and keeps quality high:

items: Annual Staff Intentions Survey: In Term 3, all staff complete a confidential survey about their plans for the following year. This gives early warning of recruitment needs.

Notice Requirements: Employment contracts state minimum notice periods (typically 90 days before the end of the academic year, or 30 days mid-year with penalties). See Section 12.4 for contract details.
Leadership Pipeline Development: Find and develop emerging leaders. Use Subject Leader shadowing, professional development opportunities, and acting roles during leave periods.
Knowledge Transfer: Departing staff complete handover documents, including curriculum plans, student information, and lists of resources. Section 12.12 sets out the exit procedures.

Rotational Staff Pool: Eduversal keeps a network-wide pool of rotational staff (teachers and managers). These staff can be sent to partner schools based on need. The GM coordinates rotational assignments; see the Juknis partnership agreements for rotation policies.
content.title: Anticipating Turnover and Succession Planning

content.text: Staffing is usually the largest operating cost (60-75% of school budgets). Workforce planning must balance educational priorities with financial sustainability:

steps.text: Annual Staffing Budget Preparation: The Principal prepares a detailed staffing budget for the following academic year, working with the GM and the Finance team. It is usually due in Term 2. This budget includes:
items: Salary and benefits for all positions (base salary, housing allowance, transportation, health insurance, pension/BPJS, professional development)
Recruitment costs (advertising, interviews, relocation support for expatriate teachers)
Work authorization and visa costs for expatriate teachers (KITAS and RPTKA/foreign-worker notification processing; see Section 2.3 for Indonesian compliance)
Substitute teacher provisions

steps: Yayasan Review and Approval: The proposed staffing budget is sent to the Yayasan Board for review and approval. The GM supports this process. The GM gives context on network-wide staffing patterns and Eduversal quality standards.

Mid-Year Adjustments: Unexpected staffing changes during the year (resignations, enrollment shifts) may require budget changes. The Principal consults the GM and the Yayasan before creating new positions or removing existing ones.

Salary Scales and Competitiveness: Salaries are compared with similar international schools in Indonesia. This helps attract and keep quality staff while respecting local economic conditions. The GM gives guidance on competitive pay packages.
content.title: Budget Considerations and Yayasan Approval

content.text: Example: A mid-sized Eduversal school has 500 students, from Primary through A Level. Such a school might employ 40-50 teaching staff and 8-12 support staff (counselors, librarian, EAL/SEN specialists, admin). It might also employ 3-5 lab/technical staff and a 4-6 person leadership team (Principal, Vice Principal, Subject Leaders). The staffing budget would include money for at least 2-3 replacement teachers each year to cover normal turnover.

content.title: SPK nationality floors — a scored accreditation requirement
items: Teaching staff (pendidik): at least 30% must be Indonesian citizens (WNI). Foreign teaching staff (WNA) may be at most 70% of the total. Source: Panduan Akreditasi SPK 2025, p.11.
Non-teaching staff (tenaga kependidikan — administration, IT, maintenance, cleaning, security): at least 80% must be WNI. WNA at most 20%. Source: Panduan Akreditasi SPK 2025, p.13.

Evidence at visitation: staff composition documents on the prescribed templates. These are form A5 and A6 (Lampiran 2) for pendidik, and form A7 and A8 (Lampiran 3) for tenaga kependidikan. Outsourced staff require the cooperation agreement as supporting evidence.

Operational consequence: check the ratio BEFORE making an expatriate offer, not at accreditation. If a school recruits to fill a subject gap without tracking the staff composition, it can fall below the minimum with no other warning. The breach is only discovered when it is scored.
Owner: the General Manager or Foundation Representative keeps the running composition figure up to date, together with the staff register.

Valid for 6 months; must be recent (within 3 months of employment start)

steps: Panel of 3: Principal, Subject Leader/HOD, HR representative or GM
Structured interview with questions set in advance (this makes it fair and consistent)
Scenarios and questions test safeguarding awareness and professional boundaries
"Describe a time when you had concerns about a student's wellbeing. What did you do?"

Candidates teach a sample lesson (15-30 minutes) or are observed during a trial day

Observe body language, tone and interactions to check that they are appropriate

If documents seem doubtful, check with the issuing institutions that they are genuine
For overseas qualifications, check equivalency through Indonesian DIKTI or international credential evaluation services
Check Cambridge training certificates with Cambridge International Education (if the candidate claims them)
All staff have a medical examination before employment
Screening for infectious diseases (TB, Hepatitis B, as set by Indonesian regulations)
Assessment of physical and mental fitness for teaching duties
Confidential. Results are shared only with HR and the Principal. They show only whether the person is fit, not specific diagnoses.

content.text:
Contract Types (per Indonesian Labor Law UU No. 13/2003 as amended by UU No. 6/2023 (Cipta Kerja) and PP No. 35/2021):

1. PKWT (Perjanjian Kerja Waktu Tertentu) - Fixed-Term Contract:

steps: Used for: new teachers (probationary period), short-term replacements, project-based roles
Duration: under PP No. 35/2021, a total of 5 years at most, including any extension or renewal. The Cipta Kerja reforms replaced the old 2+1 year rule.
After 5 years total, the relationship converts to PKWTT or employment ends
Termination: on a specific end date; by mutual agreement if it ends early
Under PP No. 35/2021, uang kompensasi (compensation pay) is due every time a PKWT expires. It is calculated pro-rata to length of service.
content.title: Employment Contracts

content.text: 2. PKWTT (Perjanjian Kerja Waktu Tidak Tertentu) - Permanent Contract:

steps: Used for: long-term teachers and staff after they pass probation or complete the PKWT cycle
Duration: no fixed end; continues until resignation, retirement, or termination with cause
Termination: requires valid reasons, due process, and severance pay per labor law
More job security; suitable for stable, experienced staff
International teachers: 1-2 year PKWT contracts (renewable), because these teachers often move between countries
Indonesian national teachers: PKWT at first, changing to PKWTT after 2-3 years of strong performance
Leadership and support staff: PKWTT for stability
Standard contracts run July-June (aligned with academic year)
State the exact start and end dates
Notice of non-renewal must be given at least 90 days before the contract ends
Mid-year contracts: prorated for the part of the year, with an option to extend

content.text: Salary and Benefits (Typical Package Components): Basic Salary:

items: Competitive with the local international school market
Based on qualifications, experience, and role complexity
Paid in IDR (Indonesian Rupiah) monthly via bank transfer
Subject to Indonesian tax withholding (PPh 21)
Monthly stipend OR school-provided accommodation
Usually 20-30% of basic salary, depending on location
May include utilities, or utilities are paid separately
Monthly transport allowance for commuting (local staff)
School may provide bus/shuttle service
BPJS Kesehatan (Indonesian national health insurance) - MANDATORY by law
The school usually provides extra private health insurance for better coverage
Coverage for employee and dependents (spouse, children)
School covers KITAS (limited stay permit) application and renewal costs

Foreign-worker authorization: the school obtains an approved RPTKA (Rencana Penggunaan Tenaga Kerja Asing, the plan for employing foreign workers). Note: the Cipta Kerja reform of UU No. 13/2003 Pasal 42 abolished IMTA. Any reference to IMTA in local practice refers to the old, replaced system. Confirm the current procedure with the Ministry of Manpower before each hire
See Section 2 for detailed KITAS procedures
Taking part in the DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency) program
Cambridge training workshops and online modules
Budget for extra PD (conferences, courses)
THR (Tunjangan Hari Raya): a mandatory religious holiday bonus of 1 month's salary for Eid al-Fitr
Performance bonus (optional; based on appraisal results and the school's financial performance)
BPJS Ketenagakerjaan (employment insurance including old-age savings) - MANDATORY
Optional private pension scheme (if available)
12-15 days of paid leave per year (in addition to school holiday periods)
Sick leave: usually 12 days per year (with a medical certificate for more than 2 days)

Maternity leave: up to 6 months under UU No. 4/2024 (Kesejahteraan Ibu dan Anak). The law guarantees 3 months, plus up to 3 more months with medical certification. Pasal 5(2) sets the wages during this leave. Pay is: full pay for the first three months, full pay for the fourth month, and 75% of pay for the fifth and sixth months. Paternity leave: 2 days paid, which can be extended under the same law
Compassionate leave: case-by-case for family emergencies
One-time payment or reimbursement for moving costs
Initial accommodation arrangement support
End-of-contract repatriation flight (for expatriates returning home)

Termination Clauses and Notice Periods:

Resignation (by employee):

items: Notice: at least 30 days for mid-year; for the end of the academic year, 90 days is preferred

Grounds: serious misconduct, safeguarding breach, gross negligence, prolonged poor performance despite support
Requires documentation, investigation, due process (warnings, improvement plans)
Severance pay may be reduced or waived for serious misconduct (under labor law)
Rare; usually used for redundancy or restructuring
Requires severance pay under UU No. 13/2003, as amended by UU No. 6/2023 (Cipta Kerja). The amount follows the PP No. 35/2021 formula (based on years of service)

Example (PP No. 35/2021 Pasal 40 ayat (2)-(3)): 1 year of service = 2 months' wages severance pay (uang pesangon). With 3 years: 4 months pesangon + 2 months long-service pay (uang penghargaan masa kerja). With 5 years: 6 months pesangon + 2 months long-service pay. Compensation of entitlements (uang penggantian hak, Pasal 40 ayat (4)) is also paid, such as untaken annual leave. For redundancy on efficiency grounds (PP No. 35/2021 Pasal 43), the pesangon multiplier is 1x where the measure prevents losses. It is 0.5x where the company is already making losses

content.text: Severance follows PP No. 35/2021 Pasal 40. Severance pay is 2 months' wages for 1 year of service, 4 months for 3 years and 6 months for 5 years (ayat 2). Long-service pay starts at 3 years of service: 2 months' wages for 3-6 years (ayat 3). Compensation of entitlements is also paid (ayat 4). UU No. 13/2003 Pasal 156 sets the same scale as a legal minimum.

content.text: KITAS (Kartu Izin Tinggal Terbatas) - Limited Stay Permit: Application Process (for new expatriate teachers):

steps: The school obtains the approved RPTKA / foreign-worker notification
The expatriate applies for a work visa (Visa 312) at the Indonesian embassy or consulate in their home country
The expatriate enters Indonesia on Visa 312
Within 7 days of arrival: apply for KITAS at the Immigration Office
KITAS is issued within 2-4 weeks (valid for 1 year at first)
Obtain an MERP (Multiple Exit-Reentry Permit). This allows the expatriate to leave and re-enter Indonesia without losing the KITAS
KITAS is renewed every year (for up to 5 years in a row)
Documents: passport, RPTKA/notification, employment contract, tax ID (NPWP), proof of address
Processing time: 2-3 weeks
School HR usually coordinates the renewal process
KITAP (Kartu Izin Tinggal Tetap) - Permanent Stay Permit
For expatriates who plan to live in Indonesia long term
Allows work without annual KITAS renewals
Requires 5 years of continuous KITAS, Indonesian language skills and recommendation letters
The school is the legal sponsor (penjamin) for the expatriate's KITAS
The school is responsible for: processing fees, document preparation and contact with immigration
The expatriate must tell the school about passport renewal, address changes and marital status changes
If employment ends, the KITAS must be canceled. The expatriate has a grace period to leave Indonesia or find a new sponsor
Expatriate income is subject to Indonesian income tax (PPh 21)
Progressive rates: 5% - 30% depending on income level
The school withholds tax from salary each month and pays it to the tax office
The expatriate must get an NPWP (tax identification number) within the first months of employment
Annual tax filing is required (March deadline for the previous year)
If employed for fewer than 183 days per year: different tax treatment applies (non-resident)

content.title: Teacher workload - Permendikdasmen No. 11/2025
content.text: Permendikdasmen No. 11/2025 tentang Pemenuhan Beban Kerja Guru sets the rules for how a teacher's workload is counted and met. Check this regulation when you set contact-hour expectations. It is also linked to the reduced load PIGP requires for a guru pemula (new teacher) in the induction year (Permendiknas No. 27/2010, Article 7). Where this manual gives contact-hour figures, confirm them against 11/2025 for the current year. Source: Permendikdasmen No. 11/2025.

editorialNotes.title: Source verification
editorialNotes.text:
Verified against the source statutes on 2026-08-16.

**PKWT duration:** PP No. 35/2021 sets "paling lama 5 (lima) tahun" (maximum five years) including extension or renewal.

**Compensation:** the same regulation establishes "Uang Kompensasi", payable on the expiry of every PKWT, calculated pro-rata to length of service.

**Maternity leave:** UU No. 4/2024 Article 4 provides "paling singkat 3 (tiga) bulan pertama" (at least three months) plus "paling lama 3 (tiga) bulan berikutnya jika terdapat kondisi khusus yang dibuktikan dengan surat keterangan dokter" (up to three further months on medical certification) - so up to six months in total.

**Paternity leave:** the same article gives the husband "cuti pendampingan istri" of "2 (dua) hari" at the birth.

**Sources:** Desktop/Eduversal Sources/hukum-umum/PP 35-2021 - PKWT, Alih Daya, PHK.pdf (salinan), no-13-2003-ketenagakerjaan.json, no-4-2024-kia.json.

[Provenance note, 2026-08-17: this regulation is NOT yet extracted into the docs/research/ archive. The citation above points to the source PDF held in Desktop/Eduversal Sources/mevzuat/, which is what was read. Extracting it into docs/research/permendiknas/ remains outstanding — until then, treat this note as a pointer to the salinan, not as an archive-backed verification.]

Note on the severance example. The example previously understated the statutory scale at every step: it gave 1 month of salary for one year of service, 2 months for three years, and 3 months for five or more years. It was corrected on 2026-08-20 against the salinan of PP No. 35/2021 Pasal 40: ayat (2) sets severance pay at 2 months' wages for 1 year of service (1 tahun atau lebih tetapi kurang dari 2 tahun), 4 months for 3 years, and 6 months for 5 years; ayat (3) adds long-service pay from 3 years of service (2 months' wages at 3-6 years); ayat (4) adds compensation of entitlements. The same scale appears in UU No. 13/2003 Pasal 156 as a statutory minimum; PP No. 35/2021 states it as the operative fixed amount.

Permendikdasmen No. 11/2025 tentang Pemenuhan Beban Kerja Guru governs how a teacher workload is counted and met. It is the instrument to check when setting contact-hour expectations, and it interacts with the reduced load PIGP requires for a guru pemula during the induction year (Permendiknas No. 27/2010, Article 7). Where this manual states contact-hour figures, confirm them against 11/2025 for the current year. This clause holds the operational detail of the teacher induction program. Clause 7.5 states the network policy on one page and points here for the operational detail. Induction Module: Teacher 26-27 remains the authority for participants. It gives the detail of what mentors and new teachers actually do. Where the wording differs, the handbook governs for participants.

Duration: Three Semesters (~18 Months) All new teachers take part in a structured induction program across their first three semesters. This includes newly qualified teachers and experienced teachers who are new to Eduversal. The program can be extended by one semester if the mentor and the school leader recommend it together. It can be shortened to two semesters on the Accelerated Track (Induction Charter v1.1; 7.5). This support helps new teachers settle smoothly into the culture, curriculum and quality standards of Eduversal Partner Schools.

Structured Support Schedule: Semester 1, weeks 1-3: daily 15-minute mentor check-ins. Semester 1, rest of term: weekly 1-hour mentor sessions. Semester 2: weekly 30-minute mentor sessions, together with the eight-touch observation cycle. End of Semester 2: every two weeks, around the Integration Checkpoint. Semester 3: monthly coaching conversations, ending with the Final Induction Completion Review.

Mentor Assignment:

steps: Every new teacher is assigned a certified mentor, usually an experienced teacher of the same subject. The mentor holds an active Eduversal Mentor Certification (valid 24 months) and supports no more than 3 mentees. Every new teacher also gets a Colleague for day-to-day settling-in
The mentor gives: guidance, encouragement, practical advice, classroom management strategies, emotional support
The mentor is NOT involved in formal appraisal (to keep trust and openness)
Mentors receive training and a modest stipend or recognition for this leadership role
content.title: Induction Framework

steps: Weeks 2-4: the mentor observes the new teacher (informal, with a developmental focus)
Weeks 5-8: the new teacher observes the mentor and peer teachers (to learn effective practices)

Months 2-9: the mentor observes one lesson each month and gives a developmental debrief the same day. This is the Observation Spine, which meets the PIGP monthly minimum. Induction observations are never F2 observations

Integration Checkpoint (end of Semester 2): the Principal, as school leader, observes one full lesson using the developmental induction rubric. This is formative, and the evidence stays inside the induction system

Final Induction Completion Review (end of Semester 3): the school leader's second checkpoint observation. It is formal but developmental, and uses the same rubric as the Integration Checkpoint. It feeds the completion sign-off. It is not tied to the probationary period, which ends by month 3 at the latest (see 12.4)

content.text: Alignment with DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency):

steps: Induction is integrated with Eduversal's DTP program
New teachers take part in DTP workshops: classroom management, lesson planning, assessment design, Cambridge curriculum
Access to online modules and resources through Educamp platform

Induction milestone records support development and transition review. They do not automatically enter appraisal or promotion scoring. Any system that logs these records must keep the evidence boundaries set in the Career Growth Framework and Induction guidance.

The induction program has eight core modules. They are delivered through a mix of workshops, online learning, shadowing and hands-on practice. Each module includes specific learning objectives, resources and evidence of completion.

content.text:
MODULE 4: Safeguarding and Child Protection (Week 2, Ongoing)

Note: This full module is for teaching staff. All new employees (including non-teaching and support staff) must complete a mandatory, role-appropriate version of safeguarding training within their first week of employment. This version focuses on core principles and reporting procedures. Section 9 gives the details.

Learning Objectives:

steps: Understand the school's safeguarding policy and legal responsibilities
Recognize signs of abuse, neglect, and wellbeing concerns in students
Know reporting procedures and low-level concerns process
Maintain professional boundaries and online safety practices
Understand safer recruitment principles (relevant for future involvement in hiring)

items: Overview of safeguarding principles: child protection is everyone's responsibility
Types of abuse: physical, emotional, sexual, neglect; also peer-on-peer abuse, bullying, online exploitation
Recognizing warning signs: behavioral changes, unexplained injuries, withdrawal, academic decline
School's safeguarding policy: read it in full; key points are highlighted
DSL (Designated Safeguarding Lead) introduction: who they are, how to contact them, when to report
Reporting procedures: record concerns on the safeguarding form (on EduNav or paper) and submit it to the DSL promptly
Low-level concerns: reporting behaviors that do not reach the abuse threshold but raise questions about adult conduct
Confidentiality and information sharing: when and how to share safeguarding information in the right way
Appropriate interactions with students: friendly but professional, avoid favorites, no physical contact except when necessary (e.g., first aid, breaking up fights)
One-to-one situations: keep door open, inform colleague, avoid isolated spaces
Social media and communication: no personal social media contact with current students; use school email/platforms only; do not share private phone numbers
Giving and accepting gifts: small tokens are acceptable (class gifts); avoid expensive or personal gifts
Transporting students: avoid it if possible; if it is necessary, have another adult present or inform the Principal
Teaching students safe internet use: privacy settings, stranger danger online, cyberbullying, digital footprint
Monitoring online platforms used in learning: Google Classroom, Zoom, LMS (make sure content and interactions are appropriate)
Reporting online safety concerns: inappropriate content, students sharing personal information, cyberbullying

content.text: Safer Recruitment (if involved in hiring in future):

items: Why background checks, reference checks and safeguarding interview questions matter
Red flags in recruitment: gaps in employment, vague references, reluctance to discuss safeguarding
Your role: observe new colleagues, report concerns about conduct, support induction process

MODULE 5: EAL and Inclusion (Weeks 4-6) Learning Objectives:

steps: Understand the needs of English as Extra Language (EAL) learners (40-70% of students in Eduversal schools)

content.text: Content: Week 4: Understanding EAL Learners and CEFR Framework:

items: English language proficiency levels: A1 (beginner) to C2 (proficient); most Eduversal students range A2-B2
CEFR can-do statements: what students can understand, speak, read, write at each level
Challenges EAL learners face: academic language vs. conversational language (BICS vs. CALP), content complexity, cultural references, processing time
Strengths EAL learners bring: multilingualism, diverse perspectives, resilience
Vocabulary pre-teaching: introduce key terms before lesson, use visuals, provide glossaries
Sentence frames and paragraph structures: "The main idea is... because..." "In conclusion, we can see that..."
Visual supports: diagrams, videos, graphic organizers, mind maps
Simplified language: break down complex sentences, avoid idioms, speak clearly and slightly slower
Collaborative learning: pair EAL learners with supportive peers, use think-pair-share strategies
Extended time for tasks: allow EAL learners more processing and writing time
Multilingual resources: dual-language dictionaries, translated instructions (when appropriate)

content.text: Week 5: MTSS (Multi-Tiered System of Support) Framework:

items: Tier 1 (Universal): High-quality, differentiated instruction for all students in mainstream classroom
Tier 2 (Targeted): Small group intervention for students needing extra support (EAL groups, reading support, math intervention)
Tier 3 (Intensive): Individualized support for students with significant needs (SEN, severe learning difficulties)
Progress monitoring: regular assessments (EASE, formative checks) to find students who need Tier 2/3 support
Collaboration with EAL Coordinator and Learning Support team

content.text: Week 6: SEN Identification and IEP Implementation:

items: Common special educational needs: dyslexia, ADHD, autism spectrum, dyscalculia, processing disorders, physical disabilities
Referral process: if you notice ongoing learning difficulties, ask the SEN Coordinator for screening/assessment
IEPs (Individualized Education Plans): individual goals, accommodations and teaching strategies for SEN students
Your role: put IEP accommodations into practice (e.g., extra time, separate room, use of laptop, reduced workload)
Communication with SEN Coordinator and parents: regular updates on progress
Students with documented SEN may qualify for accommodations: extra time (up to 25%, or over 25% where strongly justified - see 8.6), separate room, reader, scribe, use of laptop
Application process: the SEN Coordinator applies to Cambridge (with evidence). This must be done months before the exam.
Practice accommodations: students must use access arrangements in classroom assessments before the exam (to show that this is their normal way of working)

steps: Observe an EAL support lesson or co-taught class (if available)

MODULE 6: Teaching and Learning Pedagogy (Ongoing - First Term) Learning Objectives:

steps: Learn to plan and deliver effective lessons in line with Cambridge pedagogy
Build a range of questioning techniques that encourage higher-order thinking
Use active learning strategies that involve all students
Set up effective classroom management and positive behavior strategies

content.text: Content Covered Throughout Term 1 (Workshops, Observations, Practice): Lesson Planning and Delivery:

items: Lesson structure: starter/hook (engage), learning objectives (clarity), main activity (explore), plenary/closure (reflect)
Clear learning objectives: SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound); shared with students
Differentiation: planning for students with different needs (extension activities for advanced students, scaffolds for students who struggle)
Pacing: balancing teacher talk, student work and group activities; not giving too much information at once
Transitions: moving smoothly between activities, with as little wasted time as possible
Open vs. closed questions: use open questions to make students think ("Why?" "How?" "What if?")
Bloom's Taxonomy: moving from recall (remember) to higher-order thinking (analyze, evaluate, create)
Wait time: after asking a question, pause (3-5 seconds) to give students time to think
Cold calling: choose students at random to answer (not just volunteers) so that everyone stays involved
Think-pair-share: students think alone, discuss with a partner, then share with the class

content.title: Statutory basis - Program Induksi Guru Pemula (PIGP), Permendiknas No. 27/2010
items: PIGP covers every newly appointed teacher (guru pemula) at an Eduversal partner school. Article 4(c) includes non-PNS (non-civil-servant) teachers in community-run (private) schools, so SPK schools are covered too.
Teaching load (Pasal 7): a guru pemula (new teacher) teaches a REDUCED load of 12-18 contact hours per week in the induction year. This replaces the standard load stated in 12.4.

Sign-off (Pasal 9): the mentor, the head of school AND the pengawas sekolah (external supervisor) must sign the end-of-program performance assessment together. A sign-off by the school only does not meet PIGP.
Statutory rating (Pasal 9): PIGP uses the 5-category scale amat baik / baik / cukup / sedang / kurang. A rating of at least "baik" is required for the certificate.
Certificate (Pasal 9): the dinas pendidikan (local education office) issues the PIGP completion certificate, not the school. The school gives its own internal recognition separately.
Permanent appointment (Pasal 10): PIGP completion has consequences for confirmation of appointment. The school records the statutory outcome next to its own decision to confirm, extend or exit.

Boundary: the PIGP statutory rating is a compliance record. It is NOT carried into the Eduversal network appraisal score. The two systems stay separate. This follows the induction charter principle that year-one induction data never feeds network appraisal scoring.

content.title: What happens to the results
content.text: This boundary is deliberate. It is the same one stated in the Teacher Appraisal Handbook. Individual scores are shared confidentially with the teacher only. Results are never used for performance management, contract decisions or public ranking. They do not enter the teacher appraisal frameworks F1-F4, the appraisal composite or level progression. content.title: Protection for educators and education personnel - Permendikdasmen No. 4/2026
content.text: Permendikdasmen No. 4/2026 tentang Perlindungan bagi Pendidik dan Tenaga Kependidikan is the regulation on protection for teachers and education staff. It sets out the protection the state gives them in carrying out their duties. It is the counterpart to the student protections in Permendikdasmen No. 6/2026 (BSAN). BSAN protects students from kekerasan (violence), and 4/2026 protects staff. A school applies both when it handles an allegation against a staff member, a parent complaint, or a disciplinary matter involving a teacher. Check the specific procedural entitlements against the salinan (official copy) before relying on them in a live case. Source: Permendikdasmen No. 4/2026.

content.text:
Purpose of Exit Interviews: When staff resign or contracts are not renewed, an exit interview gives useful information for continuous improvement. It also keeps relationships positive.

When to Conduct:

steps: Within the last 2-4 weeks of employment
After the resignation notice is given but before the final day
content.title: Exit Interviews

steps: An HR representative OR the Principal (HR is preferred, so that the feedback is honest). If a departing staff member's concerns relate directly to the Principal or HR Manager, they will be offered another channel for their exit interview. For example, a confidential discussion with the General Manager (GM) or a designated Yayasan representative.
If the Principal holds the interview, make sure the setting is not threatening and is confidential
Why have you decided to leave?
What could have been done differently to make you want to stay?
Is there a specific incident or factor that influenced your decision?
What did you enjoy most about working here?
What were the most challenging aspects?
How would you describe the school culture and your relationships with colleagues?
Did you feel supported by school leadership and your direct supervisor?
Were your professional development needs met?
How effective was communication within the school?
Was your workload manageable?
Did you have enough time for planning, assessment, and personal wellbeing?
If you were Principal, what changes would you make?
What advice would you give to your successor?
Would you recommend this school to other teachers? Why or why not?
Hold the interview in a private, comfortable place
Explain purpose: to learn and improve, not to persuade them to stay
Promise confidentiality: feedback is shared as combined results and is not linked to any individual
Take notes; summarize key themes
Thank departing staff for their service and their honest feedback
Aggregate Data: combine feedback from several exit interviews across the academic year
Identify Patterns: look for repeated themes (e.g., workload concerns, lack of leadership support, not enough resources)
Action Plans: plan ways to deal with the issues found
Report to Leadership and Yayasan: share findings and improvement plans
Follow-Up: track whether the changes made have improved retention
Departing staff can become supporters of the school (referrals, positive word-of-mouth)
Stay connected: invite them to alumni events; ask them for references or help with recruitment
Provide positive references for strong performers (if requested and appropriate)
Celebrate contributions: farewell gathering, card signed by colleagues, recognition of achievements

Overall Responsibility: Support new teachers through the three-semester induction with guidance, encouragement and practical advice

Specific Duties:

Build a Trusting Relationship:

items: Meet the mentee regularly, following the induction phase schedule. Meet daily for 15 minutes in Semester 1 weeks 1-3. Meet weekly for the rest of Semester 1 and through Semester 2. Meet every two weeks around the end-of-Semester-2 Integration Checkpoint. Meet monthly in Semester 3.
Be approachable, non-judgmental, and supportive

Keep conversations confidential. The mentor is NOT involved in formal appraisal, so that trust is protected. This confidentiality does not cover safeguarding concerns, under any circumstances. Any child protection issue or potential safeguarding risk must be reported immediately to the Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL), following school policy.
content.title: Mentors

items: Answer questions about school policies, procedures and culture
Share practical tips on classroom management, lesson planning and assessment
Offer emotional support and encouragement during difficult moments
Observe the mentee's lessons (informal, focused on development)
Invite the mentee to observe your lessons (to show good practice)
Discuss each observation afterwards: point out strengths, suggest improvements
Help the mentee work toward induction goals (teachers are not in the appraisal cycle during induction)
Give resources and strategies, and connect the mentee with other colleagues
Speak up for the mentee's needs (extra resources, reduced duties, clearer expectations)
Tell the Subject Leader or Principal about concerns if the mentee is struggling (with the mentee's knowledge)
Reflect on your own mentoring practice; ask the mentee for feedback
Hold an active Eduversal Mentor Certification (renewed every 24 months) and take part in calibration each semester

steps: Contracts: Every employment relationship is documented in a written contract (PKWT, a fixed-term contract, or PKWTT, an open-ended contract). Contracts are in Bahasa Indonesia and registered with the Manpower Office
Teacher Certification: Teachers of Indonesian national subjects must hold, or be working toward, the Sertifikat Pendidik (national teaching certificate)
KITAS/KITAP: Expatriate teachers must have valid foreign-worker authorization (RPTKA/notification) and stay permits (KITAS). The school is the sponsor

BPJS: Enrollment in BPJS Kesehatan (health insurance) and BPJS Ketenagakerjaan (employment insurance, including old-age savings, work accident and death benefit) is mandatory. Both the school and the employee contribute

Leave Entitlements: at least 12 days of annual leave; sick leave; maternity leave. Maternity leave is 3 months guaranteed, and can be extended up to 6 months with a medical certificate (UU 4/2024; see 12.4)
THR: a mandatory religious holiday bonus (1 month salary), paid before Eid al-Fitr

Severance Pay: required for PKWTT employees who are terminated without cause. It is calculated from years of service, using the labor law formula. It is not required when a fixed-term contract ends naturally, or for termination for serious misconduct
Termination Procedures: must follow due process (warnings, improvement plans, the right to respond). Document every step. Check labor law for the specific procedures
Labor Inspections: Dinas Tenaga Kerja (the Manpower Office) may carry out inspections. Schools must keep compliant records and cooperate

content.title: Conclusion
content.text:
Good staff lifecycle management is the foundation of educational excellence at Eduversal Partner Schools. Schools attract qualified educators who share the mission. They give a full induction and ongoing professional development. They carry out fair appraisals that help staff grow. They support staff wellbeing and manage exits professionally. In this way, schools create environments where both staff and students thrive.

This Section 12 gives Principals, HR teams and Senior Leadership the frameworks, processes and tools they need. With them, they can build and keep high-performing teams of educators across the many different contexts in Indonesia.

These practices are aligned with Indonesian law, Cambridge standards and CIS/WASC accreditation requirements. When schools use them consistently, Eduversal Partner Schools continue to deliver world-class international education. This education transforms students' lives and futures.
